questions.q: What is the governing rule for choosing an isolation level?
options: Always use READ UNCOMMITTED for maximum performance
Pick the loosest level that still prevents the specific anomalies your business logic actually cares about
Match whatever isolation level a similar application uses, regardless of its own requirements
Always use SERIALIZABLE to be safe
questions.explain: Every level stricter than necessary is pure cost -- more blocking for a guarantee nothing in the code actually relies on.

questions.q: What's the recommended starting point for most everyday OLTP workloads?
options: SNAPSHOT, since it has no downsides at all
READ COMMITTED (the default), or RCSI if reader/writer blocking is a measurable problem
SERIALIZABLE, since correctness should always come first
READ UNCOMMITTED, for maximum throughput
questions.explain: READ COMMITTED prevents the one almost-always-unacceptable anomaly (dirty reads) cheaply; RCSI gives the same guarantees with less blocking, and needs no code changes.

questions.q: When should REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE actually be used?
options: Never -- they should always be avoided in production
Only for SELECT statements, never for UPDATE or INSERT
On every transaction in the application, regardless of what it does
Only when a specific, nameable correctness requirement genuinely needs the extra guarantee -- not as a default 'to be safe' choice
questions.explain: Both levels cost real concurrency, so they should be reserved for cases where you can name the anomaly (nonrepeatable read or phantom read) that would otherwise be a real bug.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does the nightly batch reconciliation job need SERIALIZABLE specifically?
options: It needs row versioning to avoid write-write conflicts
It needs to prevent dirty reads, which only SERIALIZABLE can do
It needs to block all other sessions from accessing the database entirely
A phantom row appearing or disappearing mid-run would make the open-order counts fail to match, which REPEATABLE READ cannot prevent
questions.explain: The job's exact reconciliation requirement depends on no new or removed orders slipping in between its two counts -- exactly the phantom-read gap only SERIALIZABLE closes.

questions.q: What's the best fit for reporting and read-heavy workloads that shouldn't block, or be blocked by, OLTP writers?
options: SNAPSHOT or RCSI
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.explain: SNAPSHOT and RCSI give consistent reads with no blocking in either direction, at the cost of occasionally handling a write-write conflict if the workload also writes.
